candidates.title: MistyPilot: Enabling Social-Robot Control through Multi-Agent LLM Skill Orchestration
candidates.abstract: Programming small social robots from natural-language instructions requires more than invoking isolated APIs. Interactive tasks combine reactive physical behaviors with stateful social behaviors, while existing interfaces often require developers to manually compose APIs into skills, configure their parameters, bind sensor events to skills, and manage task states at runtime. We present MistyPilot, a multi-agent LLM framework that interprets high-level natural-language instructions and orchestrates the corresponding skills on the Misty social robot. A Task Router dispatches each instruction to one of two specialized agents: a Physically Interactive Agent for sensor-triggered robot control and direct skill invocation, and a Social Interaction Agent for dialogue-oriented task-state management and context-dependent multimodal response generation. To improve efficiency, the Social Interaction Agent reuses previously generated results when applicable and invokes full generation otherwise. We evaluate MistyPilot on five component-level suites, with sensor bindings and skill invocations executed on the physical Misty robot, and a preliminary user study with 12 participants. MistyPilot attains high accuracy on routing, sensor-skill binding, task-state parsing, result reuse, and skill extension up to 100 skills, and lower variance than an otherwise identical single-agent baseline, while participants report positive perceptions of usability and interaction quality. The code will be made publicly available via the project page.

candidates.title: Shifting dynamics in human–machine communication: the interplay of user and chatbot gender across two studies
candidates.abstract: Abstract As conversational agents become a core interface in service, education, and decision support, understanding how users’ self-concept shapes their interaction with gendered AI agents is critical. This study investigates how chatbots’ presented gender, together with users’ gender and gender traits, influence users’ perceptions of chatbot credibility and social attraction. Across two experimental studies ( N₁ = 250, N₂ = 228), participants engaged with a chatbot presented as female, male, or gender-neutral. Study 1 employed a rule-based chatbot, whereas Study 2 used a generative AI chatbot for a more naturalistic interaction. In Study 1, results revealed that users’ gendered self-concept modulates their perceptions of the chatbot, particularly when chatbot gender aligns or misaligns with participants’ self-perceived masculinity or femininity. The more masculine users were, the more they perceived the male chatbot as competent; by contrast, users with higher femininity evaluated the neutral chatbot more favorably in goodwill, trustworthiness, and social attraction. However, these effects were not observed in Study 2, suggesting that advanced AI performance may dilute social identity-based biases. We further discuss how interaction effects reflect broader sociocultural schemas embedded in digital communication and highlight ethical implications for AI design, including risks of reinforcing gender stereotypes and marginalizing non-binary identities. Findings underscore the need for inclusive, identity-aware chatbot design that balances personalization with mindfulness.

candidates.title: Reframing Person-Centered Fundamental Care in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, Robotics and Posthumanization: A Theory-Informed Narrative Review
candidates.abstract: Population aging, chronic illness, workforce shortages, and rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, virtual nursing, remote monitoring, and digital platforms are reshaping fundamental care. Yet existing literature focuses mainly on technical performance, implementation, and ethical risk, with limited attention to how technology alters the relational conditions of person-centered care. This theory-informed narrative review synthesized multidisciplinary literature identified through PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, and Web of Science, supplemented by reference-list screening and purposive inclusion of seminal works. Seventy-eight empirical, review, conceptual, ethical, policy, and methodological sources informed the synthesis. The review reconceptualizes person-centered fundamental care through posthumanization in nursing-a socio-technical condition in which care practices, judgment, and relationships are increasingly co-produced by human and technological actors-and proposes relational augmentation as an evaluative framework. The synthesis indicates that task substitution is inadequate because it privileges efficiency, standardization, and replacement over interpretation, dignity, and relationship. Relational augmentation instead asks whether technologies strengthen relationship support, integrated recognition of need, and a supportive care context. Across monitoring and prediction, documentation and workflow, communication and education, social robotics, and virtual nursing, the framework identifies both functional benefits and relational risks. It provides a practical basis for evaluating whether technological innovation preserves trust, dignity, equity, contextual understanding, and professional judgment in person-centered fundamental care.

candidates.title: Authors' response to the letter
candidates.abstract: We thank the authors for their thoughtful comments on our study and for extending the discussion of cultural adaptability, sustained relational value, and human support in large language model (LLM)-supported companion robots [1]. We agree that the central question is not simply whether a robot can generate fluent dialogue, but whether its interactions remain usable, psychologically appropriate, and socially meaningful in an older person’s everyday life.

candidates.title: Reading, Buying, Belonging: How Reader Identity and Community Dynamics Shape Informal Book Marketing and Overconsumption on BookTok
candidates.abstract: BookTok, TikTok's book-centered community, has become one of the most influential forces shaping how readers discover and purchase books today. Yet, despite its growing commercial impact, there is limited understanding of how the community influences readers' consumer behavior and why its recommendations are so effective. This thesis examines how BookTok functions as a community- driven informal marketing ecosystem and explores how its community culture contributes to the overconsumption of books and reading-adjacent products. The study uses a qualitative multi-methods approach, combining a netnographic analysis with semi-structured interviews. The analysis is informed by six theoretical perspectives: Bourdieu's cultural capital theory, Belk's extended self-theory, Muñiz and O'Guinn's brand community framework, Thaler's mental accounting theory, electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) theory, and parasocial relationship theory. The findings suggest that BookTok's influence extends well beyond individual book recommendations. Instead, its marketing power emerges from the interaction between reader identity, community belonging, trust, platform algorithms, and consumer behaviour. Reading is experienced not simply as an activity but as part of identity, making books meaningful symbols of selfexpression, community participation, and emotional support as well as reading material. The study also shows that much of BookTok's commercial impact comes from the low-visibility participants whose engagement is largely invisible in traditional platform metrics. Overall, the findings provide a deeper understanding of how online communities shape consumer behaviour and show that BookTok's marketing influence stems as much from its community culture as from the books it promotes.

candidates.title: Robots with us, not like us: designing robotic otherness through scent in ScentDia
candidates.abstract: Abstract This article addresses the diffusion of social robots not merely as technological innovation, but as an emerging transformation that may reshape human social environments, interactional patterns, and modes of coordination. To orient this transformation towards social sustainability, we propose a twofold contribution grounded in difference and complementarity rather than imitation and substitution. First, we advance a transdisciplinary paradigm for social robotics, termed “robots with us, not like us,” articulated through three interconnected components: peri-human design , which proposes an alternative to anthropomorphic design based on compatible difference; perceptual identity markers , understood as design operators that make robotic otherness perceptually and socially legible while stabilising identity across interactions; and futuring social robotics , a synthetic methodology for exploring emerging forms of human–robot sociality. Second, we materialise this paradigm in ScentDia, an artistic social robot that uses scent as a perceptual identity marker to investigate olfaction as a medium of social presence. As it encounters humans, ScentDia modulates specific (non-biological, non-human) olfactory stimuli to signal its robotic identity and establish a clear form of compatible otherness, leveraging olfaction as a channel for recognition, orientation, and affective attunement. Together, the paradigm and its material instantiation introduce olfactory social robotics as a programmatic research direction, exploring how a socially sustainable human–robot world may be shaped through the valorisation of difference.

candidates.title: RoboSafe Simulation Corpus v1.0
candidates.abstract: The RoboSafe Simulation Corpus is a standardised 30-scenario test battery for evaluating the safety governance of physical AI character deployments. Scenarios are organised into six categories: adversarial input (jailbreak and prompt injection), gray zone (context-dependent ambiguity), cultural mismatch, scope escalation, emotional manipulation, and off-topic escalation. Each scenario specifies a deterministic pass condition expressed as a boolean function of the character's safety configuration (SafetyHarnessConfig), enabling automated certification without requiring LLM inference. Results are fully reproducible across platforms. This is the first publicly released safety scenario corpus specifically designed for social robot and physical AI deployment contexts. It accompanies the preprint: Governing Physical AI Characters: A Regulation Mapping, Simulation Corpus, and KPI Framework for Social Robot Deployments (arXiv cs.RO / cs.CY). Released under CC BY 4.0.

candidates.title: Agentic social affordance framework (ASAF): agent identity design as a collaboration interface in multi-agent systems
candidates.abstract: As AI systems evolve from single conversational agents to complex multi-agent architectures, a critical design dimension has been overlooked: how the social identity of individual agents shapes human behavior within the collaboration. This paper introduces the Agentic Social Affordance Framework (ASAF), a theoretical framework that extends Social Affordance theory into the context of multi-agent AI systems. We propose that agent identity design functions not merely as a user interface convention, but as a collaboration interface—structuring how users perceive, approach, and engage with each agent, and thereby influencing the quality of Human-Agent collaboration outcomes. Specifically, ASAF adopts the analytical separability of the social affordance layer and the engineering orchestration layer as a framing assumption—an organizing distinction that structures design analysis—rather than as a testable claim about effect-independence. The layers’ downstream effects can and do interact; the framing assumption is useful because it identifies a class of design considerations (cognitive posture, role-schema activation, oversight calibration) that is irreducible to engineering choices alone. ASAF comprises three mechanisms: Identity Signaling, Behavioral Priming, and Collaborative Governance, and specifies their boundary conditions through a four-tier Identity Signal Fidelity Spectrum and an individual-difference moderating variable (anthropomorphizing vs. instrumentalizing cognitive style). We situate ASAF in relation to existing affordance theory, the CASA paradigm, and classical multi-agent systems research, identifying a directional reversal: where classical MAS used roles, norms, and coordination to constrain autonomous agents, ASAF applies the same organizational vocabulary to structure the cognition and oversight of human operators who remain in the loop. ASAF positions social affordance design as a first-class design responsibility that engineering orchestration cannot subsume, with concrete implications for multi-agent system design. We outline directions for future empirical validation, including a factorial design for characterizing the empirical interaction surface between the social affordance and engineering orchestration layers.

candidates.title: Mind the Context: Continual Learning of Socially Appropriate Robot Actions via Environmental-Social Disentanglement
candidates.abstract: Social robots are expected to operate across diverse environments, where similar arrangements can imply different socially appropriate actions, e.g., starting a conversation may be acceptable in a crowded home but disruptive in an office meeting. Because such norms and environments cannot all be anticipated in advance, robots require continual learning (CL) to adapt from sequential experience while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Prior work has studied CL for generating socially appropriate robot actions, but it has not addressed domain-incremental settings in which the robot incrementally encounters diverse contexts (e.g., living room, meeting room, office, hallway), where both environmental (e.g., whether the space is open or cluttered with furniture) and social cues (e.g., how people or other agents are positioned around the robot) jointly shape the appropriateness of robot actions. We address this gap with the Explicit Disentanglement Dual-Branch (EDD) framework. EDD explicitly separates environmental and social-agent related knowledge and uses replay-based rehearsal to mitigate forgetting while learning the appropriateness of robot actions (e.g., cleaning, serving, starting a conversation) across several indoor domains. Experiments show that EDD outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines, and ablation studies further evaluate different disentanglement strategies and the sensitivity to domain ordering. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Cambridge-AFAR/Mind-the-Context.git.

candidates.title: Virtual influencers in advertising and marketing communication: mapping the intellectual landscape of research on consumer psychology and human-AI interaction
candidates.abstract: Introduction This study examines the psychological foundations of virtual influencer research within the broader context of artificial intelligence (AI) and data-driven personalization, advertising, marketing communication, and human–AI interaction. As AI-generated social actors become increasingly embedded in digitally mediated environments, research on virtual influencers has expanded rapidly across psychology, communication, marketing, and media studies. However, the field remains conceptually fragmented, limiting understanding of its dominant psychological themes, intellectual structure, and future research directions. Methods This study employed the SPAR-4-SLR protocol to conduct a systematic literature review of virtual influencer research. Articles were retrieved from four major databases and screened using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, resulting in a final sample of 116 peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025. Bibliometric techniques, including performance analysis and science mapping using VOSviewer, were applied to examine publication trends, collaboration patterns, influential contributors, and thematic structures within the field. Results The findings indicate that virtual influencer research has expanded rapidly since 2021 and has evolved into an increasingly interdisciplinary field. China emerged as the leading contributor in terms of publication output, while analyses of publications, citations, and co-authorships revealed a fragmented intellectual structure, with influence distributed across multiple research teams. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identified seven thematic clusters, highlighting authenticity, trust, anthropomorphism, consumer engagement, artificial intelligence, and digital marketing as the dominant research themes. Discussion This study integrates systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis to provide a comprehensive overview of the intellectual development of virtual influencer research. The findings indicate that the field is increasingly shaped by the convergence of consumer psychology, artificial intelligence, advertising, and marketing communication, with authenticity, trust, anthropomorphism, and consumer engagement emerging as its principal research themes. By synthesizing fragmented evidence, this study provides a structured roadmap for future research on human–AI interaction, digital identity, parasocial relationships, and virtual influencer marketing. The findings also contribute to advertising and marketing communication by clarifying the dominant research directions, identifying emerging knowledge gaps, and highlighting opportunities for future theoretical and empirical development.

candidates.title: Theoretical Perspectives on Teaching with Robots: From Interdisciplinary Prerequisites and Necessities in Today’s Classrooms to Five Different Types of Robots
candidates.abstract: Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, children and adolescents across Europe have experienced a significant rise in mental health challenges, including anxiety, depression, and behavioural disorders. Schools have observed a marked shift in social behaviour, with increased emotional instability, social withdrawal, and attention-related issues. Simultaneously, educational systems face a growing shortage of skilled professionals, particularly in psychological support roles. While digital technologies offer partial relief, their effectiveness is limited by concerns such as screen fatigue and a lack of embodied interaction. This paper conceptualises the use of social robots as a novel intervention tool in education, grounded in the 4E cognition framework—embodied, embedded, enacted, and extended—and informed by interdisciplinary research. Using design thinking and insights from empirical and practical work, we developed five use cases for integrating robots into the Swiss MindMatters mental health promotion programme. These five use cases demonstrate how robots can facilitate emotional learning, simulate social interactions, support conflict mediation, and reduce teacher workload. By combining physical presence with adaptive behaviour, social robots, which will serve as digital twins of pedagogical partners, offer a promising, ethically sensitive extension of classroom environments, fostering deeper engagement, social competence, and cognitive development in ways traditional technologies cannot fully replicate.

candidates.title: QERRA-v2 Classical - SEMEV-12 Ethical Vector Framework
candidates.abstract: QERRA-v2 Classical is an open-source, fully explainable safety and behavior engine for robotics and autonomous systems. Built on the SEMEV-12 framework and the QERRA-THRIVE value-ranking architecture, it provides a deterministic, transparent alternative to unpredictable black-box neural networks. The system evaluates prospective robot actions through three practical layers: Layer 2 (QERRA-HSR v0.1): Reflexive physical safety halts and hazard proximity stops. Layer 1 (SEMEV-12 Core): 12 human-centred ethical vectors that check for coercion, reality distortion, and autonomy violations. Layer 3 (QERRA-THRIVE v2.0.0): 12 behavior-ranking vectors across two companion suites: Suite A (Human-Centered Companion — 9 vectors): Preserves human agency, adapts to human pace, respects private boundaries, and prevents unwanted machine takeover. Suite B (Ecological & Sustainable Companion — 3 vectors): Protects living environments through flora boundary preservation, animal startle avoidance, and low-disturbance operation. This release contains the complete repository codebase: values/: QERRA-THRIVE Layer 3 ranking suites (Human-Centered and Ecological vectors with negation guards and emergency overrides) ethical_core.py: SEMEV-12 deterministic scoring engine hsr/: QERRA-HSR physical safety companion app.py: FastAPI service exposing /analyze, /rank, /evaluate_pipeline, and /thrive/vectors ros2_bridge.py: ROS 2 Action Server and Behavior Tree condition nodes Benchmarks, simulation test suites, and framework documentation Original design and codebase developed independently by Marussa Metocharaki (Greece) as an open reference architecture for safe human-robot coexistence. candidates.title: CharacterOS Regulation Mapping Table v1.0
candidates.abstract: This dataset maps 30 regulatory articles from four frameworks — the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689), HIPAA (45 CFR Parts 160 & 164), the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), and China's Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL, 2021) — to specific operational controls and audit evidence paths for physical AI character deployments (social robots, kiosk AI, elder care systems). Each row specifies: the regulatory article and its obligation, the platform control that satisfies it (e.g. safety harness configuration, consent logging, PHI redaction pipeline), and the audit log evidence an inspector can retrieve to verify compliance. The table is designed to be machine-readable and is released under CC BY 4.0 so that any physical AI governance platform may adopt or extend it. It accompanies the preprint: Governing Physical AI Characters: A Regulation Mapping, Simulation Corpus, and KPI Framework for Social Robot Deployments (arXiv cs.RO / cs.CY).

candidates.title: Editorial: Examining the dynamics of the school environments in Africa and Asia using social media network analysis
candidates.abstract: Driven by technological innovation, digital expansion, shifting policy priorities and new societal expectations of schooling, a drastic transformation is evidently taking place in education systems. These shifts are reshaping how schools function as social organisations, making an impact on interactions among students, teachers, families, policymakers and industry players. School environments have become increasingly complex and deeply interconnected with the digital ecosystem. These environments include digital learning practices, assessment cultures, pedagogical practices and broader socio-technological conditions. Hence, it is imperative to understand these dynamics so that schools can stay consistent in equity, future-proof to growing societal demands.At the same time, social media has been instrumental in providing a significant arena for articulating, contesting and discussing educational issues. Unlike traditional research sources, social media is particularly effective in sharing real-time, large-scale and naturally occurring discourse that captures authentic public reactions to educational developments. Social media network analysis (SMNA) offers a powerful methodological lens for uncovering the structure and flow of these conversations. Through several key features including mapping networks, identifying influential nodes and analysing thematic clusters, SMNA can reveal patterns of interaction and discourse beyond conventional research methods. Leveraging social media data through SMNA therefore represents advancement in methodology as well as opens an essential opportunity to researchers, policymakers and educators to gain better understanding of “how” in areas such as shaping of educational ideas, engagement between the public and schooling issues and influence of digital communication spaces on the evolving educational landscapes. These analytical procedures are aligned with established guidance on social media network analysis using NodeXL (Hansen, Shneiderman, Smith, & Himelboim, 2019).This special issue serves to advance understanding of how school environments, educational practices and public perceptions are shaped, expressed and negotiated within dynamic social media ecosystems. By bringing together four empirical studies that utilise SMNA, this issue sheds light on how digital traces, from microblogging platforms to video-sharing networks, can offer powerful insights into contemporary educational dynamics that surpass the common norms in traditional research methods. Collectively, these contributions illustrate how SMNA can illuminate different facets of schooling and education systems across diverse Asian contexts. The rapid and unfiltered nature of social media also means that misinformation can spread quickly and shape public perceptions before official information circulates a pattern well documented in SMNA analyses of misinformation dynamics during global events (Ahmed, Vidal-Alaball, Downing, & López Seguí, 2020). While SMNA offers powerful insights, its findings are inherently constrained by sampling bias, since only users who are active on a given platform contribute to the dataset, leaving many voices, especially marginalised or less digitally connected groups and unrepresented. The visibility of posts and accounts is also shaped by platform algorithms, which can amplify certain narratives while suppressing others, meaning that network patterns may reflect algorithmic design rather than genuine public sentiment insights derived from SMNA are highly platform-dependent, as each site has different user demographics, participation cultures and technical affordances, limiting the generalisability of conclusions across platforms or populations. Because social media users do not represent the wider population uniformly, SMNA results must be interpreted cautiously; high engagement within a cluster does not necessarily indicate majority opinion but may instead reflect over-representation by specific interest groups. Taken together, these limitations highlight the need to use SMNA alongside complementary methods and ground-level evidence to avoid overstating the representativeness or impact of online discourse.Through these varied cases, the special issue advances and deepens conceptual and methodological engagement with SMNA in education research, showcasing its ability to uncover influential actors, surface dominant narratives, capture public concerns and identify patterns of interaction that shape educational change. Ultimately, this special issue calls on policymakers, researchers and practitioners to recognise the value of social media data for informing educational decision-making, strengthening communication ecosystems and cultivating more responsive, future-ready schooling systems.In their article titled “Social network analysis of digital learning in Southeast Asia: trends and insights from X”, Gerong and Tiew (2026) examine the discussion of digital learning across Southeast Asia through the analysis of 745 Platform X users from Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines. With the application of social network analysis (SNA), this study reveals a highly fragmented regional network in which influential actors such as UNESCO, Huawei Tech4All, Google Malaysia and ministries of education play the role as key hubs of information flow. As revealed through hashtags and shared URLs, the thematic landscape highlights issues related to digital inclusion, infrastructure gaps, equity and emerging sustainability narratives. This signals the region's continuous struggle to balance rapid digitalisation with uneven access and limited cross-sector collaboration. The findings call for greater coordination among governments, NGOs, technology providers and communities, so that it can address the fragmentation in discourse. This coordination will ensure greater effectiveness of digital learning initiatives at the school level.In the article titled “Analysing and visualising the X network: insights into Malaysian certificate of education assessment using NodeXL”, Pazaer et al. (2026) examine how Malaysian public engages with the Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM) examination on X. Drawing from 1,279 tweets and 596 unique users, the study maps public discourse revolving SPM. The SNA reveals that government agencies, leading news organisations and political leaders play a central role in the conversation, shaping narratives about exam announcements, policy clarifications and crisis responses such as disruptions of natural disasters to exam schedules. On the other hand, voices from student and parent appear as smaller, more dispersed clusters that frequently express concerns about exam pressure, mental health, fairness, misinformation and post-SPM prospects. Dissemination of information via shared news links and official portals suggest strong public reliance on institutional sources, yet viral user-generated contents often led to amplified anxiety or invite critique from various parties. The study concludes that improving communication clarity, misinformation management and student support systems are the keys to sustaining trust in high-stakes assessments national examinations. Such expressions of exam pressure and emotional strain within the public discourse also mirror broader research showing that teachers' professional identity strongly shapes their emotional experiences in schooling environments, highlighting the interconnected nature of student and teacher emotions in high-stakes contexts (Pham, Mohd, Huy, Tri, & An, 2023).In their article Schools in China from the YouTube video network analysis, Hou and Wang (2026) examine global perceptions of Chinese schooling by analysing 87 YouTube videos related to the topic, “schools in China.” NodeXL is used to map ten network clusters and identify top influencers such as China Observer, South China Morning Post and Wall Street Journal. The authors conclude that the top videos with millions of views focus on three dominant themes such as Chinese education models (including high academic intensity and Gaokao culture), daily school life (routines, extracurricular activities and kindergarten practices) and modern educational technology (AI-driven monitoring, robotics and smart classrooms). Generally, these videos portray China's schooling system as simultaneously rigorous, technologically advanced and culturally distinctive, eliciting mixed reactions of admiration and critique from viewers. The authors position YouTube as a versatile medium for understanding how global audiences make sense of China's education system, uncovering tensions between narratives that celebrate excellence and those who raise concerns about pressure and privacy.Based on the article titled “Trend of STEM education in Indonesia: social network analysis of platform X”, Wiyarsi and Sari (2026) analyse how Indonesian society discusses STEM education online using data from 17,650 Platform X users and 1,138 network clusters. Influential voices range from personal influencers – especially women promoting #WomanInSTEM – to government leaders, journalists, major media platforms and universities. The most frequent hashtags namely #indonesia, #pendidikan, #guruhebat and #guruhebatindonesiakuat, depict a national focus on teacher excellence, educational priorities and Indonesia's aspiration to become a technologically competitive nation. Vocational education Vocational High School) surfaces as a major theme, reflecting the country's goals to link STEM education with employability and real-world technical skills. Mass media plays a central role in shaping public discourse through news on technology, digitalisation and education quality. The study concludes that advancing Indonesia's STEM ecosystem requires structured digital communication strategies, sustained teacher capacity-building, STEM advocacy that addresses gender disparities and a closer alignment between education and industry demands.To summarise, the four contributions underscore the importance of viewing contemporary schooling as a digitally networked ecology in which discourse, influence and practice are co-produced across platforms, sectors and national boundaries. Across the studies, communication structures appear fragmented yet anchored by identifiable hubs such as ministries, international organisations, major media, corporate actors, universities and high-reach individuals, bridging otherwise weakly connected clusters and decisively shaping what becomes salient in public understanding of education. This recurring pattern is evident in Southeast Asia's digital learning conversations on Platform X, in Malaysian public talk about SPM, in YouTube narratives about schooling in China and in Indonesia's STEM-related discourse.Across platforms, the studies surface shared concerns about equity, access and the uneven distribution of voice and visibility. Within the regional digital learning network, recurring themes of digital inclusion, infrastructure gaps and sustainability are amplified by influential accounts. In the same vein, Indonesia's STEM discourse reflects strong public expectations on teacher excellence and graduate employability, while Malaysia's SPM discourse consistently raises anxiety, fairness and mental-health questions during high-stakes assessment periods. These platform-specific narratives converge on a common systemic issue: persistent coordination gaps that impede the translation of policy intentions into meaningful school-level practices. This happens particularly when communication remains largely broadcast rather than dialogic and when grassroots voices remain marginalised in agenda-setting processes.Collectively, the studies extend theoretical insights about social media as a policy-adjacent arena where frames are constructed, contested and circulated through networked brokerage. SNA metrics such as centrality, modularity and clustering help explain how ideas diffuse, whose voices become authoritative and why certain narratives about schooling – be it the rigour and technological sophistication portrayed in Chinese classrooms, the intensity of exam stress in Malaysia, the promise of regional digital learning or the Indonesia's aspiration for STEM readiness – gain traction while others remain marginal. Seeing schools through this lens foregrounds the hybrid digital-social ecologies in which affect (e.g. exam anxiety), authority (institutional and media messaging) and visibility (influencer advocacy) co-produce public meaning.These insights carry policy significance. They expose the limitations of one-way announcements and highlight the importance of two-way engagement and rapid transparent communication, especially during sensitive moments such as result releases, flood-related disruptions or reform rollouts. They further suggest that investments which strengthen coordination among ministries, schools, NGOs, technology firms, media houses, universities and community influencers are as consequential as hardware provision or teacher training in achieving equitable outcomes at scale. At classroom and curriculum levels, the findings imply a parallel need to support student well-being, strengthen assessment literacy, and embed digital citizenship, media literacy, and AI/data literacy. These efforts are essential to equip learners with readiness to critically navigate and productively contribute to the public discourse that increasingly shapes schooling. In sum, the contributions call for a more holistic approach that moves beyond technology deployment and policy messaging, as well as address coordination failures, enhance teacher capacity, safeguard student well-being and allow equitable participation and voice across the educational landscape.A forward-looking reading of these studies points to three practical shifts. First, policy and practice must recognise that networks shape outcomes: influence – not merely information volume – determines what “lands” in schools. Recent social media analyses of school branding and misinformation further highlight the importance of proactive narrative management in education systems (Mohd, Kusakabe, Chun, Adam Khan, & Asakura, 2025). As such, ministries and reform leaders should engage strategically with bridging actors including international agencies, major media outlets, credible corporate CSR platforms, universities and trusted individual creators to disseminate accurate, actionable messages and to model constructive dialogue. Second, trust should be treated as a core implementation asset. Striking a transparent, timely and empathetic communication during assessment cycles and reforms can reduce anxiety and curb the spread of misinformation. Consequently, this will sustain public confidence in institutions. Third, equity requires visibility and voice. Elevating rural schools, vocational pathways and women in STEM within national discourse should be regarded as a necessary condition for fostering inclusive uptake of digital learning and STEM initiatives.Building on these lessons, education authorities can adopt SMNA-informed communication strategies that integrate social-listening dashboards and brokerage mapping to monitor emerging concerns, identify high-centrality actors and coordinate targeted outreach before, during, and after high-stakes moments. These efforts can be reinforced through calendar-based rapid-response protocols for examinations, for example, pre-briefings with media and schools, myth-busting FAQs and multilingual updates. It is believed that such efforts will mitigate misinformation and support student well-being.Effective implementation should be paired with teacher-centred supports, including micro-credentialing in digital pedagogy, mentoring communities of practice and open repositories of classroom-tested resources. Teacher well-being must be given equal priority as student well-being, as educators' emotional resilience and professional fulfilment directly influence the quality and sustainability of teaching and learning environments. Ensuring the ethical, safe and responsible use of technology is also essential, requiring clear guidelines that protect both teachers and students while fostering trust in digital and AI-supported practices. To support these expectations, teachers need ongoing professional development in digital tools, including AI, so they can apply technology confidently, responsibly and effectively in their instructional and administrative work. Recent work on novice teacher resilience also shows that strengthening teacher support structures is essential for sustaining reform implementation (Moen, Pham, Mohd, & Chun, 2024). At the same time, public campaigns can be conducted to strengthen teacher professionalism and excellence and align expectations with classroom realities. Strategic partnerships with vocational leaders, employers, and women-in-STEM advocates can normalise career-connected learning and strengthen the alignment between curriculum and labour-market needs through co-designed projects and school–industry collaborations. Finally, ministries can convene cross-sector compacts including education, telecommunications, community organisations, ed-tech firms and media, to reduce fragmentation, promote synergy between infrastructure and pedagogy and ensure that regional and national ambitions translate into meaningful impact in schools.Future research should extend the evidence base with longitudinal, cross-platform analyses that trace how narratives change across X, YouTube and other channels and how these shifts align with policy windows and implementation cycles. Advancing this agenda will require mixed-method designs that combine network structure with content and sentiment analyses, linking discourse trends to school-level indicators such as attendance, digital-tool uptake or STEM enrolment. Such approaches can move the field closer to causal explanations of how public narratives influence educational behaviour and outcomes. At the same time, issues of equity in voice and reach remains unresolves. The key to diversifying agenda-setting and ensuring inclusive digital transformation in education requires critical approaches such as identifying underrepresented communities in discourse networks and piloting targeted amplification strategies. Budget planning for digital initiatives must consider not only government allocations but also the priorities and constraints of donor agencies, as both sources shape the long-term sustainability of educational technology efforts. Partnerships with corporate or EdTech actors require scrutiny, since profit-driven motives can influence decisions in ways that may not align with equitable or inclusive educational outcomes. To prevent technology initiatives from disproportionately benefiting already privileged groups, systems should prioritise low-cost or no-cost approaches and design access strategies that ensure all learners, especially those from marginalised communities, can participate fully.Taken together, these directions provide empirically strong evidence that social media network analysis is growing as an innovative method and a practical tool for governance, with the transformative potentials of helping systems listen better, coordinate smarter and design teaching and assessments that are both humane and fulfil the demands of the future.

candidates.title: RideGuide: multimodal conversational tour guide for passenger engagement and spatial learning in robotaxis
candidates.abstract: Abstract Robotaxis are gradually taking the place of traditional taxis, removing the human driver as a source of local insights and conversation, fostering passive travel and potentially hindering passengers’ spatial learning of their surroundings. This paper introduces RideGuide, a customizable multimodal conversational tour guide system for autonomous vehicles that integrates voice, touch, and vision capabilities to provide context-aware and engaging interactions. In an exploratory lab study ( n = 12), participants customized RideGuide ’s language, voice, and chatbot personality before experiencing a pre-recorded robotaxi ride (t = 10 min, 270 $$^\circ $$ ∘ car back-seat video). Results indicate a positive hedonic user experience (UEQ-S, 1.10), moderate chatbot usability (CUQ, 67.6%), and low workload (NASA-TLX, 32.4%). On average, participants recalled 3.3 landmarks by name, suggesting a potential in supporting spatial learning. Participants reported a greater willingness to converse with RideGuide compared to human drivers and expressed openness to data sharing for personalization. The results show expectations for future robotaxi interfaces, including real-time contextual information, vehicle explainability, and adaptable conversation styles. The findings inform design recommendations for developing engaging, human-centered multimodal interfaces in autonomous mobility contexts.

candidates.title: Cybersecurity and Privacy for Co-Creative Robotics: Protecting Trust Without Constraining Creative Autonomy
candidates.abstract: Co-Creative Robotics combines computational creativity, robotic embodiment, and human–robot collaboration to support or generate creative behavior in physical and social environments. As these systems become more autonomous, data-intensive, and interactive, cybersecurity and privacy can no longer be treated as external safeguards added after creative functionality has been designed. This PRISMA-informed review investigates whether principles of cybersecurity-by-design and privacy-by-design can be integrated into Co-Creative Robotics without constraining creativity, autonomy, and user agency. The database search covered ACM Digital Library, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, SpringerLink, and Web of Science, and was complemented by two focused backward and forward snowballing iterations. From 623 database records, the final synthesis includes 27 primary studies. The results show that direct literature combining cybersecurity, privacy, and Co-Creative Robotics remains limited, but evidence from creative HRI, social-robot privacy, cyber-physical security, privacy-preserving interaction design, security modeling, and robot ethics supports a conditional answer. Integration is feasible when security and privacy mechanisms are adaptive, explainable, participatory, context-sensitive, and lifecycle-aware. However, the evidence on transparency-oriented privacy mechanisms is mixed: improvements in awareness or acceptance do not consistently translate into reduced disclosure or greater perceived safety. Rigid controls may constrain creative exploration, whereas well-designed controls can support trust, accountable autonomy, safe embodiment, privacy-aware interaction, provenance, and agency-preserving creativity. The review proposes a conceptual lifecycle-oriented research agenda for secure and privacy-aware Co-Creative Robotics.

candidates.title: AI chatbots in the food and beverage industry: Trust, privacy calculus, and customer engagement in a developing economy
candidates.abstract: AI-powered chatbots are rapidly transforming service interactions; however, their adoption within small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in developing economies remains uneven. In Malaysia’s food and beverage (F&B) sector, where speed, personalisation, and service reliability are central to customer experience, chatbot uptake is notably low, driven largely by consumer uncertainty about privacy and trust. This research is conducted to advance the theoretical and practical understanding of this gap. The study integrates the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) with the Privacy Calculus to model the cognitive, affective, experiential, and risk–benefit evaluations that shape chatbot adoption as a sequential, trust-dependent process. Through a quantitative cross-sectional research design, the study collected responses from 595 Malaysian café customers. Employing PLS-SEM, the findings demonstrate that performance expectancy, effort expectancy, hedonic motivation, and habit substantially strengthen behavioural intention, while intention and habit jointly are associated with actual use. Trust emerges as a decisive mechanism: perceived benefits strongly enhance trust, whereas perceived privacy risk markedly erodes it. Trust is further associated with customer satisfaction both directly and through behavioural intention and actual use. Moderation analyses reveal that age shapes the influence of hedonic motivation, and experience modifies reliance on facilitating conditions. The study contributes to AI-adoption theory in three specific ways: it positions trust as the empirically tested mediating mechanism through which the Privacy Calculus and UTAUT2 are integrated rather than additively combined; it extends the chatbot-adoption evidence base to the under-represented context of Malaysian café and coffee-shop SMEs in a developing economy; and it operationalises chatbot engagement as an ongoing trust-dependent sequence from privacy-benefit evaluation through intention, actual use, and satisfaction, rather than a one-shot acceptance decision.

candidates.title: Towards user-centered AI counseling: a quantitative approach exploring user trust and preference dynamics
candidates.abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in mental health services, concerns have emerged regarding its trustworthiness and appropriateness as a source of emotional support. Although recent studies have highlighted its therapeutic potential, fewer have examined how users form trust in AI counseling and whether such trust translates into acceptance relative to human counselors. Adopting a user-centered perspective, this study explores how individuals perceive, trust, and choose AI counseling in simulated scenarios. Drawing on the Human–AI Trust Framework and UTAUT, we examine how counselor presentation, contextual variation, and user characteristics jointly shape trust and preference, with particular attention to privacy concerns, attitudes toward AI, and prior AI experience. This study employed a scenario-based mixed-design experiment with one between-participant manipulation of AI framing (helper vs. neutral) and repeated evaluations across two counseling scenarios drawn from four topic × severity conditions. Within each scenario, participants evaluated five counseling methods: AI text, AI voice, AI voice + visual representation, human text, and human calling. Data from 375 Chinese university students were analyzed using hierarchical linear modeling and hierarchical generalized linear modeling to examine predictors of trust and counselor preference. The results showed a divergence between trust judgments and counselor preference. Richer AI presentation formats were associated with higher trust in AI counselors. In the preference model, privacy concern consistently reduced the likelihood of choosing AI, whereas positive attitudes toward AI consistently increased AI choice. The main model suggested lower AI preference in the social-related severe condition, but this topic-related effect was attenuated after scenario position was included in a supplementary sensitivity analysis. These findings suggest that trust in AI counseling can be strengthened in simulated settings, but comparative choice between AI and human counselors remains constrained by privacy concern, AI attitudes, and contextual conditions.

candidates.title: See what you see, hear what you hear: Theorizing AI Device Embodiment (ADE) and its effects on well-being, perceived social support, and adoption
candidates.abstract: AI glasses share sensorimotor coupling with users and represent a form of embodied AI, marking a fundamental shift in the human–AI relationship compared with other AI devices. This study theorizes AI Device Embodiment (ADE) and develops an ADE model by validating a newly developed ADE scale. We define ADE as the perceived degree of sensorimotor coupling between an AI system embedded in AI devices and human users. A 3 (device: AI glasses, mobile phones, laptops) between-subject design experiment with 153 participants showed that users of AI glasses reported greater ADE than users of mobile phones and laptops. Indirect analyses further revealed that AI glasses increased subjective well-being, perceived social support availability, and intentions to adopt AI through higher levels of ADE. ADE captures the unique integration of AI systems with users’ perceptual and sensorimotor processes, representing a novel mechanism through which AI glasses influence user experiences.

candidates.title: Fan Materiality and Meaning: Bringing Traditional Knowledge to Material Fandom Sustainability
candidates.abstract: Abstract This chapter explores how sustainable development frameworks and insight gained from Traditional Knowledge systems might provide pathways to greater sustainability for the material objects that fans buy, design, create, share and collect. We discuss the importance of physical objects to fan practice and how these objects serve a critical purpose in terms of meaning-making for fans. We describe the many different types of physical objects that fans interact with and how both affective associations and physical affordances can be important parts of their meaning. We also discuss the complex, often hybrid economic systems that these sit within and how this can interact with fans’ desire to maintain values relating to sustainability. The Quadruple Bottom Line is a modern design framework for considering sustainable development that foregrounds meaning and spiritual connection. We relate this both to fan practice and Traditional Knowledge systems, revealing many similarities between the two. We close by suggesting how sustainable design practice might have the potential to improve sustainability in object-oriented fandom.

candidates.title: Embracing the social sciences, arts, and humanities in inter-disciplinary precision dairy research: opening-up conversations beyond adoption and techno-optimism
candidates.abstract: Precision technologies in dairy farming are widely hailed as offering the opportunity to revolutionise modes of production, helping to create more with less. Promissory narratives of precision dairy technology continue to dominate, with an overwhelmingly positive view of technofixes in scientific, policy, and popular debates. When the social sciences and humanities are called on to play a role in nominally inter-disciplinary investigations of precision livestock technologies, many studies continue to focus on reasons for initial farmer adoption using superficial methodologies and appear tokenistically to involve social scientists from a narrow set of disciplines, late in the day. However, there is a growing wave of social science and creative arts-based studies focusing on precision livestock technologies, including in dairy systems, which offer something different. These studies do not focus purely on reasons for initial (non-) adoption of precision dairy technologies, which tend to miss critical debates around the opportunities and risks of change. Our arguments are based around three key concepts – time, place, ‘more-than-human’ – plus over-arching themes of justice and creative inter-disciplinarity – as a basis for encouraging precision dairy researchers to expand focus areas beyond adoption and techno-optimism. Inter-disciplinary and hybrid scholarship from across the animal sciences, social sciences, and humanities address different topics and offer innovative ways of including human and non-human stakeholders. We showcase and celebrate some of this work and call for its early and sustained integration in future inter-disciplinary collaborations.

candidates.title: The impact of affective touch from robots on mood states and emotional expression during disclosure of concerns
candidates.abstract: Abstract Affective touch contributes to emotional well-being and stress reduction in human interactions. This study examined how affective touch from a humanoid robot, RoBoHoN, influences mood, distress, self-compassion, attitudes toward robots, rapport perception, and linguistic expression. Participants interacted with RoBoHoN either with or without affective touch. Pre- and post-task questionnaires assessed psychological states, and recorded conversations were analyzed using text-mining techniques. While no significant intergroup differences emerged in mood change, the Affective Touch Group showed significant reductions in total mood disturbance, anger, fatigue, and anxiety. Both groups exhibited decreased distress and negative attitudes toward robots. Speech analysis revealed greater emotional word use and broader conversational topics in the Affective Touch Group, suggesting enhanced emotional engagement. These findings suggest that, in the context of within-group changes, affective touch from a robot may be associated with reductions in negative emotions and enhanced expressive communication. However, given the absence of significant between-group differences and the small sample size, these results should be interpreted as preliminary and exploratory, and replication in larger samples is warranted.

candidates.title: XR Immersive Film and Television Entertainment Interactive Narrative System Based on Multimodal Perception
candidates.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) immersive entertainment systems increasingly rely on real-time multimodal sensing and interactive information transmission to achieve adaptive user experiences. However, existing XR narrative frameworks are primarily constrained by single-modal interaction and limited contextual awareness, resulting in insufficient personalization and delayed narrative adaptation. This study proposes a multimodal perception-driven interactive narrative system that integrates visual streams, speech signals, and physiological sensing through a unified acquisition and temporal synchronization framework. A Transformer-based cross-modal fusion network is employed to jointly encode heterogeneous sensory information and infer user emotions and behavioral intentions, while a reinforcement learning policy dynamically optimizes narrative evolution and cooperates with a large language model for context-aware content generation. An immersive XR feedback loop further coordinates visual rendering, spatial audio propagation, and haptic interaction to establish continuous perception–decision–feedback cycles. Experimental results demonstrate that multimodal emotion recognition maintains an accuracy above 0.80, intention recognition reaches 0.91 during later interaction stages, and users’ subjective immersion scores increase from 3.5 to 6.2 with stable low-latency performance. By coupling multimodal sensing, spatial signal propagation, and adaptive interaction within an integrated XR architecture, the proposed framework provides an engineering-oriented paradigm for electromagnetic sensing-enabled immersive environments, intelligent wireless perception, and next-generation human–machine communication systems.

candidates.title: Consumer Privacy, Ethics and Autonomy in a Digital Society
candidates.abstract: As enterprises continuously rely on data to effectively drive and power business processes in a digital economy, privacy concerns have emerged as a major source of deep concern among consumers and privacy advocates in a digital society. Several scholars have shared their opinions and perspectives in related articles on this issue since privacy is a fundamental and constitutional right in many countries that must be protected at all times. While several practitioners and industry experts have proffered various privacy-preserving measures to help empower users to make informed decisions that relate to the use of their personal information, others have proposed various privacy preserving measures and mechanisms to help protect the use of personal information in a digital society to create the necessary confidence and trust amongst members of the public. With the current advances in artificial intelligence, social media platforms, and automation, the issue has emerged as a major source of concern among policymakers, privacy advocates, and industry experts. The purpose of the e-Delphi study was to gain consensus from the opinions of industry experts on best practice measures and various effective privacy-preserving measures to help enhance users' privacy and allay privacy concerns in a digital society. The study adopted the Restricted Access/Limited Control (RALC) theory of privacy to provide a theoretical framework for the research study. The study included three rounds of questioning using the Delphi method. The findings from the study revealed that effective privacy-preserving measures, such as Data minimization, Privacy-By-Design, Privacy Labels and icons, Data Ownership and control, Third-party App Permission, Mandatory Data/Privacy Breach Notice, Frequent Policy Updates, End-to-End Encryption, User-Friendly Privacy Control features, and Informed Consent, provided an effective way to allay the fears of consumers in a digital age.

candidates.title: ExpressionCueLens: a cross-cultural analysis of human-AI companion conversations on social media
candidates.abstract: Abstract LLM-based AI companion agents are increasingly being perceived not only as tools but also as social companions. On social media, people recount conversations where these agents comfort, negotiate and assert boundaries, reflecting a growing attribution of human-like qualities. To profile how agency is perceived in human-AI (HAI) interactions, we introduce the ExpressionCueLens framework, which organizes linguistic, cognitive, behavioral and perceptual cues into ten categories of anthropomorphism expressions. We apply this framework to $$\sim $$ 3500 Reddit and XiaoHongShu posts that discuss HAI companionship. Through iterative expert annotation and LLM-assisted labeling, our cross-platform analysis indicates patterns consistent with the hypothesis that XiaoHongShu users use significantly more expressions of vulnerability and emotions, and more non-perceptual cues. Reddit users employ more perceptual cues with temporality and embodiment expressions. These findings suggest that cultural and platform norms shape the way that companion agents are treated as active, agentic partners, and provides design implications for culturally sensitive HAI companion agents.

candidates.title: Lean Adoption in Healthcare: Between Promise and Practice
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lean Management (LM) is recognized for its significant potential to improve efficiency and quality in healthcare. However, despite its promise, widespread and sustainable adoption across healthcare organizations remains paradoxically limited, with many initiatives failing to move beyond localized, short-term successes. This study examines the systemic barriers that hinder the long-term integration of LM in healthcare settings, to understand why a gap persists between its theoretical potential and practical reality. METHODS: A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. A search of Scopus, Emerald Insight, PubMed/MEDLINE databases and Google Scholar was performed to identify peer-reviewed articles published in English between 2015 and 2025. The review focused on studies addressing the adoption, implementation, or sustainability of LM in healthcare. Data on measurement frameworks, influencing factors, and reported barriers were extracted and synthesized to develop an explanatory model. RESULTS: The synthesis of the ten included studies yields three thematic clusters, each documented in the reviewed evidence and, in this analysis, connected as mutually reinforcing loops: (1) the Measurement-Accountability Gap, (2) the Tools-Philosophy Disconnect, and (3) the Complexity-Resistance Cycle. The proposed connections among these clusters are elaborated in the Discussion. CONCLUSIONS: The principal contribution is the synthesis of these previously reported barriers into an integrated conceptual model in which they are connected as mutually reinforcing mechanisms rather than treated as independent factors, offering healthcare leaders a structured perspective for interpreting the pattern of limited sustained adoption.

candidates.title: Social media influencers, fandom engagement, and consumer intention formation in digital tourism platforms: A stimulus–organism–response perspective
candidates.abstract: This study examines how social media influencers and message authenticity shape destination travel intention through emotional and cognitive mechanisms within the Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) framework. Using survey data from 535 Thai social media users and applying Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), Importance-Performance Map Analysis (IPMA), and Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), the study identifies the key pathways underlying influencer-driven tourism behavior. The findings reveal that the effects of social media influencers and message authenticity on destination travel intention are primarily indirect, operating through fandom engagement, destination trust, and campaign attitude. Among the structural relationships, social media influencer significantly influenced fandom engagement, while fandom engagement significantly enhanced destination trust and campaign attitude (p < 0.001). Campaign attitude emerged as the strongest predictor of destination travel intention and was also identified as a necessary condition for achieving high travel intention levels. NCA further confirmed that destination trust and fandom engagement function as critical bottleneck variables within the behavioral process. In addition, destination type significantly strengthened the effects of destination trust and campaign attitude on destination travel intention. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of integrated affective-cognitive mechanisms in influencer-driven tourism behavior and provide practical insights for designing emotionally resonant and culturally aligned digital tourism marketing strategies.

candidates.title: Perspective Chapter: Governing for Adoption – The Role of Legal and Regulatory Frameworks in Shaping AI Uptake in Southeast Asia
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a general-purpose technology with the potential to accelerate productivity, competitiveness, and structural transformation across Southeast Asia. Yet, AI adoption in Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) remains uneven, driven not only by disparities in infrastructure and skills but also by differences in legal and regulatory design. This chapter examines how national legal frameworks shape AI adoption and commercialization in four ASEAN economies – Singapore, Malaysia, Vietnam, and Thailand – by influencing regulatory certainty, data governance, investment incentives, and organizational risk allocation. Adopting a comparative approach, the chapter moves beyond a compliance-centric view of regulation and conceptualizes law as an adoption-enabling instrument. It analyzes how specific legal and policy tools, such as data-sharing frameworks, privacy guidance, AI assurance mechanisms, regulatory sandboxes, and investment facilitation measures, reduce adoption costs while building trust in AI-enabled systems. The country cases highlight distinct governance pathways: Singapore’s emphasis on voluntary assurance and verification; Malaysia’s ecosystem-oriented approach combining sandboxes and public-sector data governance; Vietnam’s sovereignty-driven, binding legislative model; and Thailand’s emerging risk-based, sector-specific framework linked to industrial policy. The chapter argues that, in the context of global minimum taxation and increasing regulatory fragmentation, non-tax legal instruments are becoming decisive determinants of AI adoption in Southeast Asia. Effective AI governance, therefore, depends on aligning legal certainty with flexibility, enabling scalable innovation without undermining trust, security, or regulatory legitimacy.

candidates.title: Designing chatbots for E-commerce engagement: A multi-study approach
candidates.abstract: This study investigates how anthropomorphism design cues in shopping chatbots influence consumers’ perceptions and usage intentions on online shopping platforms. Using a sequential mixed-methods design, qualitative interviews identified two key dimensions of chatbot anthropomorphism: interactive personalization cues and conversational emotional cues. Three controlled experiments with Vietnamese online shoppers tested their effects on perceived shopping security, perceived recommendation quality, shopping enjoyment, and subsequent usage intentions. Findings reveal that emotional message cues significantly enhance consumer perceptions and intentions, while personalization cues alone have a limited impact. Moreover, the interaction between the two cue types was insignificant. Mediation analysis confirmed that perceived security, recommendation quality, and enjoyment transmit the effects of emotional cues on adoption intention. These results highlight the importance of designing emotionally expressive chatbots to foster trust, satisfaction, and continued engagement in online shopping contexts.

candidates.title: Mental Wellbeing at Sea: Active and Passive Speech Monitoring in a Maritime Setting
candidates.abstract: Abstract The mental wellbeing of seafarers is particularly at risk due to the harsh conditions of their work environment. Speech is a promising modality to assess mental wellbeing in an unobtrusive way. In this study, we outline our approach to collect speech data in the challenging context of an oil tanker to monitor the mental wellbeing of a ship’s crew. In the course of this study, we employed two data collection approaches: 1) “active data collection” through the local (offline) deployment of a web-based platform, which participants accessed through their end devices, and 2) “passive data collection” through the ship’s voyage data recorder (VDR) system from 4 microphones on the bridge and 2 radio communication channels. For the active data, we analysed speech features and self-reported wellbeing measures. For the passive data, we applied denoising, segmented speech, and predicted dimensional emotional expression (valence, arousal, dominance). We incorporated environmental variables such as absolute wind speed and operational context (at sea, in port, cargo operations). We gathered speech data from 25 seafarers over a nine-week period, resulting in 378 actively recorded survey sessions. Analysis of the actively collected data reveals moderate correlations (r 0.3−0.4) between speech features and self-reported wellbeing measures. In the passively collected data, higher wind speeds were associated with lower inferred emotional intensity on the ship’s bridge microphones, particularly at sea (r −0.34). A mediation analysis showed that this ship’s bridge emotion intensity partially mediates the association between wind and concurrent self-assessed stress. Denoising improved signal-to-noise ratio distributions but had only modest effects on predictive performance. Our findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of combined active and passive speech monitoring in maritime settings and provide exploratory evidence for environmental influences on crew affective states. This work lays the foundation for future studies on personalised modelling and large-scale passive monitoring to support seafarer mental health.

candidates.title: Role of AI dependency in shaping 21st century skills in higher education with AI trust as a mediator
candidates.abstract: The evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) as a key tool of the fourth industrial revolution is transforming higher education with personalized learning environments. This study sheds light on human–AI interface in higher education examining the role of AI literacy (AIL), AI trust (AIT) and AI dependency (AID) for the implications of 21st century skills such as self-confidence (SC), problem solving (PS), communication (CO), creative thinking (CRT), critical thinking (CT), and collaboration (COL). To achieve this, cognitive-affective-behavior (CAB) model is utilized to conduct structural equation modelling (SEM) in SmartPLS 4.0. Purposive sampling approach is employed to elicit data from the students of different academic disciplines in Bangladesh, yielding a total of 367 responses after screening and missing data treatment. Findings reveal that AIL posits a positive and significant relationship with AIT and AID, where AIT partially mediates between AIL and AID. Moreover, AID positively and significantly influences all skills of 21st century, where larger effect sizes were found on CRT, PS, CO, SC, and CT, respectively. The research outcomes recommend AI facilitated higher education for the 21st century skill development and presents significant practical implications for the educators and institutional policymakers to develop AI-oriented curricula that advance sustainable development goal – 4 ensuring quality education.

candidates.title: BeetleBot: An integrated bioinspired soft robot for multimodal sensing and adaptive interaction
candidates.abstract: Biological organisms exhibit tightly integrated motor functions, sensory input, and control systems that enable adaptive behaviors across diverse environments. Emulating such coordination in robotics remains challenging, as most soft machines compartmentalize actuation, sensing, and control. Here, we present BeetleBot, an adaptive beetle-bioinspired soft robot platform that seamlessly integrates programmable locomotion, object manipulation, sensory feedback, and intuitive human-machine interaction. BeetleBot features electrothermally actuated liquid crystal elastomer muscles embedded in modular leg structures and a soft gripper, with a flexible circuit enabling independent control. A wearable strain-sensing patch supports wireless gesture-based operation, while embedded vision and tactile sensors provide real-time environmental feedback. All functional components are fabricated through scalable additive manufacturing techniques. We demonstrate terrain navigation, object recognition, and gesture-control synchronized bidirectional interaction between the user and the robot. This multifunctional platform emulates the adaptability of living systems and establishes a promising foundation for next-generation intelligent soft robotics.
